h1: The 5 Best Immersion Blenders Under $150 for Soups and Sauces, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 immersion blenders under $150 from Breville, Braun, KitchenAid and Ninja, compared on speed control, attachments and grip.
summary: The Breville Control Grip is the immersion blender to buy if soups, purees and sauces are your weekly routine, because it is the only one here built around a trigger grip that adjusts speed with your hand. The Braun MultiQuick 7 is the best kit for cooks who want a chopper and whisk in the same box, and the Braun Vario 5 is the strongest pick for fine speed control on a mid-range budget. The KitchenAid suits owners who like attachments, while the Ninja is the compact choice for small jobs.
intro: Most people buy an immersion blender by counting accessories, then end up using the stick alone for years. The part that decides whether you enjoy the tool is the one you touch every time: how the motor starts, how speed is controlled, and how easily the blending head clears a pot of hot soup without splattering the stove.

This ranking looks at five hand blenders that sit under the $150 ceiling, drawn from the Breville, Braun, KitchenAid and Ninja lines. We reviewed each one from its listed specifications, accessory list and brand track record, and we ranked them on control, kit value and how well they fit real kitchen jobs. Where a listing leaves out a detail, we say so instead of filling the gap.

products.name: Breville BSB510XL Control Grip Immersion Blender
products.verdict: A brushed stainless stick with a squeeze-to-speed grip that rewards cooks who blend every week.
products.description:
The Control Grip is Breville's take on the classic stick blender, finished in brushed stainless steel and built around a grip that lets your hand set the pace. The listing sits in the $100 to $200 bracket, which makes it the priciest model here and also the one aimed most squarely at people who cook from scratch.

It ranks first because speed control is the feature that separates a pleasant blender from a frustrating one. Pressing harder to go faster means you can start slowly in a deep pot of hot liquid and ramp up once the ingredients are moving, which cuts the splatter that a single full-speed button invites. Against the Braun MultiQuick 7 below it, the Breville gives up the extra food processor attachment, and that is the honest tradeoff: you are paying for feel and finish, not for a pile of accessories.

Buy it if you puree soup, make sauces or blend smoothies several times a month and want something that feels solid in the hand. Skip it if you want a chopper bowl and whisk in the box, since the listing does not advertise either.
pros: Grip lets your hand set speed
products.idealFor: Home cooks who puree soups and sauces every week.
products.skipIf: You want a full attachment kit for the money.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 7 3-in-1 Immersion Blender & Food Processor
products.verdict: A three-in-one bundle that turns the blender into a small food processor for $50 to $100.
products.description:
The MultiQuick 7 packs a hand blender and a food processor attachment into one bundle, which is why it is listed as a 3-in-1. It lands in the $50 to $100 bracket and carries Braun's reputation for sturdy, plainly engineered kitchen motors.

It ranks second because the accessory value is real. A chopper bowl handles onions, herbs, nuts and breadcrumbs, jobs that the stick alone does badly, so a small kitchen can skip buying a separate mini processor. It sits behind the Breville since the Breville feels more refined in use, but it beats every other model here on how much it replaces. The drawback of any bundle is storage: the bowl, lid and blades take drawer space and add more parts to wash.

This is the pick for a first immersion blender or a small apartment where one appliance has to do three jobs. Think twice if you only ever blend soup, because you would be paying for pieces you will leave in the cupboard.
pros: Braun motors have a sturdy reputation
cons: More pieces to wash after use
products.idealFor: Small kitchens that need one tool for many jobs.
products.skipIf: You only blend soup and never chop.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick Vario 5 Hand Blender
products.verdict: A 500W stick with 21 speeds and a turbo button, good for cooks who like fine control.
products.description:
The Vario 5 is a straightforward hand blender with a 500W motor, 21 speed settings and a turbo boost button. It sits in the $50 to $100 bracket and focuses on the stick rather than a pile of extras.

It ranks third because 21 speeds give you a wide dial between a slow stir and a hard blend, which matters when you move from a delicate cream soup to a thick hummus. Turbo covers the stubborn lumps. It trails the MultiQuick 7 on kit value, since the listing sells the blender itself rather than a bundle, and it trails the Breville on the feel of its control. Watch the wattage figure: 500W is a respectable number for home use but it is not a measure of how smooth the result will be, because blade design does as much work as the motor.

Buy it if you want precise speed steps and a lower price than the Breville. Skip it if you expect a chopper or whisk, which the listing does not mention.
cons: Control less intuitive than a grip
products.idealFor: Cooks who want a precise dial on a budget.
products.skipIf: You want a chopper or whisk included.

products.name: KitchenAid Variable Speed Corded Hand Blender with Attachments KHBV83
products.verdict: A corded variable-speed blender sold with attachments, for owners who like the KitchenAid look.
products.description:
The KHBV83 is a corded, variable-speed hand blender sold with attachments, priced in the $50 to $100 bracket. It brings KitchenAid's familiar styling and the idea of a kit that grows with your cooking.

It ranks fourth because the listing is vaguer than the Braun and Breville entries: it names the attachments in general terms but does not give a motor wattage or a speed count to compare. A corded design also keeps power consistent through a long pot of soup, which battery stick blenders often cannot do, so the cord is a plus for heavy jobs. The cost is that you must stay near an outlet and manage the lead around a hot stove.

Choose it if you already own KitchenAid appliances and want a matching kit. Skip it if you compare machines on published numbers, because this one gives you fewer of them.
pros: Corded power holds through thick soups
cons: Cord limits reach around the stove
products.idealFor: KitchenAid owners who want a matching attachment kit.
products.skipIf: You want published wattage and speed counts.

products.name: Ninja Immersion Blender & Whisk CI201ND
products.verdict: A 4-speed blender with a whisk and a 4oz cup, handy for small batches and light jobs.
products.description:
The Ninja CI201ND pairs a four-speed blending stick with a whisk and a 4oz cup, in a deep navy finish. It sits in the $50 to $100 bracket and aims at small, quick tasks.

It ranks last because four speeds give a coarser range than the 21 settings on the Braun Vario 5, and a 4oz cup is a sample size rather than a working vessel. Still, the whisk is a practical addition for whipped cream or eggs, which a bare stick cannot do. The compact format is the real draw: it stores easily and costs less effort to clean than the larger kits above.

Buy it for occasional sauces, dressings and baby-food portions, or as a second blender for a dorm or a rental. Skip it if you regularly blend large pots of soup, because the small cup and limited speed range will frustrate you.
cons: Cup is too small for batches
products.idealFor: Small kitchens and occasional sauce or dressing makers.
products.skipIf: You blend big pots of soup often.

whatMatters.factor: Speed control that matches your recipes
whatMatters.detail: Speed control is how the blender ramps from a gentle stir to a hard blend. A trigger or grip, as on the Breville, lets you start slow in a deep pot and build up, while a 21-step dial like the Braun Vario 5 lets you pick a set pace. On a listing, look for a stated speed count or a variable control, and be wary of a single on-off button if you plan to make hot soup.

The bell at the bottom of the shaft keeps food moving toward the blades and prevents the head from sealing against a pot floor. A good guard also protects nonstick cookware from scratches. Listings rarely spell this out, so check whether the pictures show a wide, vented bell and a detachable shaft for washing.

Wattage tells you how hard the motor can work, but it does not tell you how smooth the result will be, because blade shape matters as much. A corded model keeps full power through a long batch, whereas a cordless one can fade. Compare listed wattage where it is given, as with the 500W Vario 5, and treat a missing figure as a reason to read further.

A chopper bowl and whisk are the add-ons that earn their space, since they handle onions, nuts and whipped cream that the stick cannot. Extras beyond that tend to gather dust. Check which pieces ship in the box and ask whether you would otherwise buy a separate mini processor.

A detachable shaft rinses under the tap in seconds and often goes in the top rack of a dishwasher, which keeps you using the tool. Bundles add bowls and lids that need a drawer. Look for a clear note that the shaft detaches and that parts are washable.

faq.q: Can I use an immersion blender in a nonstick pot?
faq.a: Yes, but keep the guard clear of the pot floor and sides, because a spinning head can scratch the coating. Lift the blender slightly off the bottom while it runs. If you cook mostly in nonstick, lean toward a model with a wide protective bell.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when using a stick blender?
faq.a: Lifting the head out of the liquid while it is running. This throws hot soup across the stove and walls. Switch the motor off first, and start at a low speed until the head is submerged.

faq.q: Is the Breville worth it over the Braun models?
faq.a: If you blend regularly, the grip control and stainless build make everyday use more pleasant. If you want a chopper bowl and want to spend less, the Braun MultiQuick 7 gives more for the money. For casual cooks the Braun is the safer value.

faq.q: Do I need a food processor attachment?
faq.a: Only if you do not already own a mini chopper. The attachment handles onions, nuts and herbs, which a plain stick cannot. If your counter is full, a bare blender is simpler to store and wash.

faq.q: How should I clean a hand blender?
faq.a: Detach the shaft, rinse it under warm water right after use and run a drop of dish soap through the head in a tall glass. Never submerge the motor body. Dry the shaft before storing it.

faq.q: Are corded or cordless blenders better?
faq.a: Corded models keep their power steady through thick soups and large batches, which is why most of this ranking is corded. Cordless ones are more convenient but can lose strength as the charge drops. For heavy jobs, corded is the safer call.

finalTake: For a cook who blends regularly, the Breville BSB510XL Control Grip is the best immersion blender here thanks to its grip-based speed control and stainless build. The Braun MultiQuick 7 is the smart pick when you want a food processor included, while the Braun Vario 5 wins on fine speed control for less. The KitchenAid KHBV83 suits attachment fans and the Ninja CI201ND handles small jobs on a tight budget. Decide whether control or accessories matter more, and the choice becomes easy.
